title: The magical number seven, plus or minus two: Some limits on our capacity for processing information
authors: George A. Miller
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Summarised evidence that the immediate memory span of young adults is about seven items
Emphasised that effective capacity can be extended by recoding/chunking
practical_applications: Historical anchor only; use Cowan's ~4 chunks as design ceiling
limitations: Not read; 'seven' described by later authors as partly rhetorical

title: The magical number 4 in short-term memory: A reconsideration of mental storage capacity
authors: Nelson Cowan
key_findings: When rehearsal and long-term-memory chunking are prevented, a single central capacity limit averages about 4 chunks (population range about 3 to 5)
Miller's 7 reflects rehearsal and grouping; capacity is counted in chunks, not raw items
Some theories place the limit in duration/decay rather than number (debated in the article)
practical_applications: Max ~4 meaning units per slide/shot
Lists of 3-4 items; group longer lists into categories
Limit new names/numbers per spoken sentence
limitations: Lab tasks with digits/words/shapes, not narratives
Defining a 'chunk' in real sentences is hard

title: Gorillas in our midst: Sustained inattentional blindness for dynamic events
authors: Daniel J. Simons; Christopher F. Chabris
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Many observers engaged in an attention-demanding counting task failed to notice an unexpected person in a gorilla suit
Noticing depends on primary-task difficulty and on similarity of the unexpected event to attended items
practical_applications: Give price/CTA its own moment, not during long captions or main action
limitations: Read via search summaries only; feed-context magnitude unknown

title: Faces and text attract gaze independent of the task: Experimental data and computer model
authors: Moran Cerf; E. Paxon Frady; Christof Koch
key_findings: In free viewing, faces were fixated ~16.6x and text ~11.1x more than comparable regions (size/position normalised)
Participants found it hard to avoid faces and text even when costly
Adding face/text channels to a bottom-up saliency model improved fixation prediction
practical_applications: Place the product near faces/text, which capture gaze first
Text in speech bubbles is the gaze magnet for faceless Mint & Tao
limitations: Static desktop images; no cartoon or faceless characters tested

title: Individual differences in face salience and rapid face saccades
authors: Maximilian Davide Broda; Petra Borovska; Benjamin de Haas
key_findings: 77 participants: saccades were faster to faces, face features and text than to cars; the advantage was largest for full faces
Isolated eye regions were not sufficient to produce face-like rapid saccades
Stable individual differences in face saccade speed, weakly correlated with face fixations in free viewing
practical_applications: Full faces beat partial faces for instant capture; text also has a speed advantage
limitations: Lab saccadic choice task, not a feed

title: Gaze cueing of attention: Visual attention, social cognition, and individual differences
authors: Alexandra Frischen; Andrew P. Bayliss; Steven P. Tipper
key_findings: Reviews the gaze-cueing paradigm: observers shift attention in the direction another face is looking
Covers social-cognitive, developmental and clinical individual differences
practical_applications: Have the model look at the glasses or key text at least once
limitations: Only abstract read; effect sizes not extracted

title: Motion onset captures attention
authors: Richard A. Abrams; Shawn E. Christ
key_findings: Across three experiments, the onset of motion (not motion per se) captured attention
Debated: Franconeri & Simons argued some motion captures attention by itself; a later account linked the effect to jerky animation (disputed)
practical_applications: Stagger element entrances so the key element starts moving alone
limitations: Abstract only; simple lab displays

title: Top-down and bottom-up control of visual selection (Acta Psychologica 135) - read only via Egeth, Leonard & Leber commentary
authors: Jan Theeuwes
key_findings: (Per commentary) Theeuwes argues an initial feedforward sweep is stimulus-driven so salience dominates early orienting; top-down control acts afterwards
Commentators argue capture is much smaller when target and distractor are known in advance, implying some top-down control
practical_applications: Make the first frame win on salience alone
limitations: Target article itself not read; only commentary snippet

title: Top-down versus bottom-up attentional control: a failed theoretical dichotomy
authors: Edward Awh; Artem V. Belopolsky; Jan Theeuwes
key_findings: The goal vs salience dichotomy is inadequate; selection history (past selections/rewards) also shapes an integrated priority map
practical_applications: Keep series visual identity stable so followers' selection history works for us
limitations: Abstract level; later debate continues on terminology

title: Cognitive architecture and instructional design: 20 years later
authors: John Sweller; Jeroen J. G. van Merrienboer; Fred Paas
key_findings: Reviews 20 years of cognitive load theory: manage load so processing irrelevant to learning is minimised and germane processing optimised within capacity
Grounds the theory in evolutionary psychology and extends it to course-level design and measurement
practical_applications: Cut extraneous load: split-attention, redundancy, transient information
limitations: Full text not reached (login redirect); effects come from instructional settings

title: Research-based principles for designing multimedia instruction (chapter in: In Their Own Words, APA Division 2)
authors: Richard E. Mayer
key_findings: Median effect sizes from Mayer (2021): multimedia d=1.35 (13 tests); coherence 18/19 d=0.86; signaling 26/28 d=0.70; redundancy 8/12 d=0.10; spatial contiguity 9/9 d=0.82; temporal contiguity 8/8 d=1.31; segmenting 7/7 d=0.67; pre-training 10/10 d=0.78; modality 18/19 d=1.00; personalization 13/15 d=1.00; voice 6/7 d=0.74; embodiment 16/17 d=0.58; image 7 tests d=0.19; generative activities 37/44 d=0.71
Redundancy effect diminishes or reverses when the lesson is slow/learner-paced, on-screen text is short or reworded, learners use a second language, or there are no graphics

Signaling works best used sparingly, for low-knowledge learners and complex material; coherence strongest for low working-memory learners, system-paced lessons and highly interesting extraneous material
practical_applications: Captions with VO are acceptable (small redundancy cost); keep any extra on-screen headline to keywords
Place text next to what it describes; sync narration with visuals
Use a conversational script and the most human-sounding TTS voice
limitations: Author's own meta-analysis of mostly his lab's studies; outcome is learning transfer, not engagement

title: The past, present, and future of the cognitive theory of multimedia learning
authors: Richard E. Mayer
key_findings: Reviews four decades of CTML; core ideas (dual channels, limited capacity, active processing) constant over time
Lists 15 evidence-based multimedia design principles
practical_applications: Framework for clip and carousel design reviews
limitations: Abstract/introduction level only

title: Meta-analysis of the modality effect
authors: Paul Ginns
key_findings: 43 independent effects; strong modality effect (spoken text + graphics beats written text + graphics), especially under system-paced conditions
practical_applications: In clips (system-paced) let voice carry the explanation while visuals show
limitations: Abstract only; moderators not extracted

title: Verbal redundancy in multimedia learning environments: A meta-analysis
authors: Olusola O. Adesope; John C. Nesbit
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Spoken+written presentations outperformed spoken-only; condensed on-screen key words added to narration were associated with better learning; negative effects most likely when spoken and written text are identical and accompanied by pictures
practical_applications: Subtitles are not harmful for short social clips; on-screen headlines should be condensed keywords
limitations: Not read beyond secondary summaries

title: Cognitive load theory and the effects of transient information on the modality effect
authors: Wayne Leahy; John Sweller
key_findings: Longer audio text was inferior to equivalent visual text (modality effect reversed) because transient speech overloads working memory; shortening the audio restored the usual modality effect (modality x length interaction)
Earlier paper (Leahy & Sweller 2011, Applied Cognitive Psychology 25(6):943-951) reported the same reversal
practical_applications: Keep VO sentences short; move dense facts to persistent on-screen text or visuals
limitations: Abstract only; sample sizes unverified

title: A meta-analysis of how signaling affects learning with media
authors: Sascha Schneider; Maik Beege; Steve Nebel; Gunter Daniel Rey
key_findings: (Secondary summary) 103 studies, 12,201 participants; retention g+=0.53, transfer g+=0.33
Benefit larger for low prior knowledge learners; moderated by pacing and signal type
practical_applications: One clear highlight per slide; design for novices
limitations: Numbers from secondary sources, not checked against original

title: A meta-analysis of the segmenting effect
authors: Gunter Daniel Rey; Maik Beege; Steve Nebel; Maria Wirzberger; Tobias H. Schmitt; Sascha Schneider
key_findings: 56 investigations, 88 comparisons: segmenting has small-to-medium effects on retention and transfer, lowers overall cognitive load and increases learning time
High prior knowledge learners gained more retention from segmentation
practical_applications: One story beat per slide; clear segment breaks in clips
limitations: Abstract only

title: A review of research and a meta-analysis of the seductive detail effect
authors: Gunter Daniel Rey
key_findings: Existence and bibliographic data confirmed; Mayer (2023) cites it for coherence boundary conditions (stronger when extraneous material is highly interesting)
practical_applications: Remove interesting-but-irrelevant decorations
limitations: Content not read

title: Keep it coherent: A meta-analysis of the seductive details effect
authors: Narayankripa Sundararajan; Olusola Adesope
key_findings: Existence confirmed (Educational Psychology Review, 2020); cited by Mayer (2023) as support for the coherence principle
practical_applications: Same as Rey2012
limitations: Content not read

title: Processing fluency and aesthetic pleasure: Is beauty in the perceiver's processing experience?
authors: Rolf Reber; Norbert Schwarz; Piotr Winkielman
key_findings: The more fluently an object is processed, the more positive the aesthetic response; figural goodness, symmetry, figure-ground contrast, repetition and prototypicality all raise fluency
Fluency is hedonically marked and used as information unless attributed to an irrelevant source (then discounted)
Figure-ground contrast affected prettiness only at short exposures (0.3-3 s), not at 10 s (Reber & Schwarz 2001, as reported)
Same statements judged more likely true in high contrast (Reber & Schwarz 1999, as reported); repetition increases both liking and truth judgments
practical_applications: High text/background contrast and readable fonts for feed viewing
Consistent, recognisable brand style
Do not exploit repetition for unsupported health claims
limitations: Theoretical review; preference for complexity explained via attribution, not directly tested

title: Uniting the tribes of fluency to form a metacognitive nation
authors: Adam L. Alter; Daniel M. Oppenheimer
key_findings: Reviews fluency as a general metacognitive cue influencing judgments across perceptual, linguistic and conceptual forms
practical_applications: Simple wording and clear layout make claims feel truer and nicer - use responsibly
limitations: Abstract only

title: The truth about the truth: A meta-analytic review of the truth effect
authors: Alice Dechene; Christoph Stahl; Jochim Hansen; Michaela Wanke
key_findings: 51 studies; repetition increases judged truth: d=0.39 within-items, d=0.50 between-items (random effects)
A 2021 registered report notes original data unavailable and that bias correction might give smaller effects
practical_applications: Ethics: never use repetition to push unproven claims
limitations: Search-summary level; meta-analysis quality questioned

title: Disfluent fonts don't help people solve math problems
authors: Andrew Meyer; Shane Frederick; et al.
key_findings: Pooling the original experiment with 16 replications: no effect of hard-to-read fonts on solution rates under any tested condition; disfluent fonts only slightly slowed responses
practical_applications: Never use hard-to-read fonts as a 'make them think' device
limitations: Abstract only; specific to reasoning problems

title: Levels of processing: A framework for memory research
authors: Fergus I. M. Craik; Robert S. Lockhart
doi_isbn: Journal of Verbal Learning and Verbal Behavior 11:671-684
key_findings: (Secondary summaries) Memory depends on depth of processing at encoding, from shallow sensory to deep semantic analysis; offered as a framework, not a complete theory
Criticised for not defining depth independently of memory outcome
practical_applications: Make jokes/messages hinge on meaning, not just visuals
limitations: Not read in full

title: Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention
authors: Henry L. Roediger III; Jeffrey D. Karpicke
key_findings: Restudy beat testing at 5 minutes, but prior testing produced substantially better retention at 2 days and 1 week, even though restudy raised confidence more
practical_applications: End carousels with a question to answer before the reveal
limitations: Abstract only; educational prose, not ads

title: Distributed practice in verbal recall tasks: A review and quantitative synthesis
authors: Nicholas J. Cepeda; Harold Pashler; Edward Vul; John T. Wixted; Doug Rohrer
key_findings: 839 assessments in 317 experiments: spaced beats massed; the optimal inter-study interval grows with the retention interval
practical_applications: Re-surface key health messages across episodes days/weeks apart in new forms
limitations: Abstract only; verbal recall in lab

title: Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology
authors: John Dunlosky; Katherine A. Rawson; Elizabeth J. Marsh; Mitchell J. Nathan; Daniel T. Willingham
key_findings: Practice testing and distributed practice rated high utility; elaborative interrogation, self-explanation, interleaving moderate; summarisation, highlighting, keyword mnemonic, imagery for text, rereading low
practical_applications: Prefer retrieval prompts over repeated summaries
limitations: Abstract/press-release level

title: Chunking mechanisms in human learning
authors: Fernand Gobet; Peter C. R. Lane; Steve Croker; Peter C-H. Cheng; Gary Jones; Iain Oliver; Julian M. Pine
key_findings: Distinguishes deliberate, goal-oriented chunking from automatic perceptual chunking; illustrated with verbal learning, expert memory and language acquisition
practical_applications: Keep a fixed episode/slide structure so followers chunk the format
limitations: Abstract only

title: Mental models and human reasoning
authors: Philip N. Johnson-Laird
key_findings: People reason by building models of possibilities; models represent what is true and omit what is false, reducing working-memory load but producing systematic errors
practical_applications: Keep character world rules consistent; use one correct comparison visual for lens functions
limitations: Abstract level; reasoning theory applied to narrative by analogy

title: Whatever next? Predictive brains, situated agents, and the future of cognitive science
authors: Andy Clark
key_findings: Examines the hierarchical prediction-machine view of the brain as a candidate unifying account of perception and action, and lists evidential, methodological and conceptual challenges
practical_applications: Craft metaphor only: set up an expectation before a twist
limitations: Theory; abstract level

title: The free-energy principle: a unified brain theory?
authors: Karl Friston
key_findings: Proposes that free-energy minimisation (an upper bound on surprise) accounts for action, perception and learning and may unify several brain theories
practical_applications: Do not cite as scientific proof in published content
limitations: Highly theoretical and contested; abstract level

title: Unification by fiat: Arrested development of predictive processing
authors: Piotr Litwin; Marcin Milkowski
key_findings: Argues PP's status as a unifying theory is asserted rather than earned; gaps between theory and its biological/computational bases have arrested its development
practical_applications: Treat predictive processing as low-confidence theory
limitations: Abstract level

title: Perception of intersensory synchrony: A tutorial review
authors: Jean Vroomen; Mirjam Keetels
key_findings: Reviews measurement of audiovisual synchrony (temporal order and simultaneity judgments) and ways the brain handles lags: wide integration window, compensation, recalibration of perceived synchrony, shifting one stream toward the other
practical_applications: Sound slightly late is tolerated more than sound early
limitations: Search summary only; numeric windows not read here

title: Temporal window of integration in auditory-visual speech perception
authors: Virginie van Wassenhove; Ken W. Grant; David Poeppel
key_findings: 43 participants: audiovisual speech integration spans an asymmetric window of about 200 ms favouring visual lead; speech tolerates larger asynchrony than non-speech
Later work cites roughly 50 ms audio-lead to 200 ms visual-lead as perceived synchronous
practical_applications: Lip-sync: mouth may start slightly before audio, never audio clearly before mouth
limitations: Abstract and citing sources only

title: The construct of the multisensory temporal binding window and its dysregulation in developmental disabilities
authors: Mark T. Wallace; Ryan A. Stevenson
key_findings: Defines the temporal binding window as the span within which multisensory inputs are likely integrated; the window is altered in autism, dyslexia and schizophrenia and is malleable
practical_applications: Expect individual differences in sync tolerance; aim inside the tightest thresholds
limitations: Abstract level

title: Recommendation ITU-R BT.1359-1: Relative timing of sound and vision for broadcasting
authors: International Telecommunication Union, Radiocommunication Sector (ITU-R)
key_findings: Subjective tests: detectability thresholds about +45 ms (sound advanced) to -125 ms (sound delayed); acceptability about +90 ms to -185 ms
practical_applications: Never let audio lead picture by more than ~45 ms (about 1 frame at 30 fps)
limitations: Read via quoted search snippets of the official text; broadcast TV tests from the 1990s

title: Embodied Cognition (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
authors: Lawrence Shapiro; Shannon Spaulding
key_findings: Cognition is embodied when deeply dependent on bodily features beyond the brain; distinguishes embodied from embedded and extended cognition; critics argue the body's role may be causal rather than constitutive
practical_applications: Use bodily acting for characters; avoid strong claims about body-to-mind effects
limitations: Search snippets only; archived edition

title: Registered Replication Report: Strack, Martin, & Stepper (1988)
authors: Eric-Jan Wagenmakers; et al.
key_findings: 17 labs, same protocol: pen-in-teeth vs pen-in-lips cartoon funniness difference 0.03 points (95% CI -0.11 to 0.16) vs 0.82 in the original
practical_applications: Do not claim 'just smile and you'll be happy' as science
limitations: Abstract level

title: A multi-lab test of the facial feedback hypothesis by the Many Smiles Collaboration
authors: Nicholas A. Coles; et al.
key_findings: 3,878 participants in 19 countries: facial mimicry and voluntary smiling amplified and initiated happiness; pen-in-mouth evidence less conclusive; lead author notes the effect is small
practical_applications: Eye-break clips may invite a relaxed face but must not overclaim
limitations: Abstract/press level

title: Eye movements when reading spaced and unspaced Thai and English: A comparison of Thai-English bilinguals and English monolinguals
authors: Heather Winskel; Ralph Radach; Sudaporn Luksaneeyanawin
key_findings: Thai sentences with inserted interword spaces were read slightly slower (1834 vs 1746 ms, marginal) with more fixations (9.27 vs 8.62, significant) than normal unspaced Thai
Spaces facilitated recognition of target words but did not change initial landing positions in Thai; removing spaces severely disrupted English
Authors suggest Thai-specific segmentation cues (e.g. vowel letters written before the consonant, tone marks) may guide skilled readers
practical_applications: Do not insert spaces between every Thai word in slides or captions; break lines at phrase boundaries
limitations: Single-line sentences on desktop; bilingual university readers

title: Eye movements while reading an unspaced writing system: The case of Thai
authors: Benjawan Kasisopa; Ronan G. Reilly; Sudaporn Luksaneeyanawin; Denis Burnham
key_findings: 30 Thai adults: higher position-specific frequency of word-initial and word-final characters moved landing sites closer to word centre, suggesting readers use character-position statistics for eye guidance
practical_applications: Use common spelling; avoid unusual abbreviations that break familiar word boundaries
limitations: Search summary only

title: Adding spaces to Thai and English: Effects on reading
authors: Chananda Kohsom; Fernand Gobet
doi_isbn: Proceedings of the 19th Annual Conference of the Cognitive Science Society, 388-393
key_findings: Thai readers were faster and made fewer errors with added spaces; meaning helped independently; no transfer of unspaced reading skill to English (not eye-tracking)
practical_applications: Conflicts with Winskel 2009 - treat spacing advice as medium confidence
limitations: Conference paper; abstract only

title: Viewers can keep up with fast subtitles: Evidence from eye movements
authors: Agnieszka Szarkowska; Olivia Gerber-Moron
key_findings: 74 English/Polish/Spanish viewers at 12, 16, 20 cps: comprehension and scene recognition unaffected by speed
Share of time on subtitles rose ~50% to ~60% (Exp.1) and ~40% to ~45% (Exp.2) from slow to fast
Slow subtitles caused far more rereading (about 2 in 3 vs 1 in 5) and more frustration; interviews suggested synchronisation mattered more than speed
practical_applications: Do not over-slow Thai subtitles; prioritise precise sync with speech
limitations: European languages, not Thai; speed confounded with text reduction

title: Don't throw away your printed books: A meta-analysis on the effects of reading media on reading comprehension
authors: Pablo Delgado; Cristina Vargas; Rakefet Ackerman; Ladislao Salmeron
key_findings: 54 studies (2000-2017, ~171,000 participants): comprehension better on paper than screens in both between- and within-subject designs
Screen inferiority larger for expository texts and under time limits (as summarised by later review)
practical_applications: Keep informational carousels shorter than narrative ones
limitations: Abstract/summaries; mostly longer texts than our slides

title: Headlines, pictures, likes: Attention to social media newsfeed post elements on smartphones and in public
authors: Anna-Theresa Mayer; Jakob Ohme; Ewa Maslowska; Claire M. Segijn
key_findings: Eye-tracking, 201 students, dynamic Facebook newsfeed: less attention to visuals on mobile; in public settings more attention to textual post elements
practical_applications: Always pair images with a short text carrying the message
limitations: Search summary only; student sample; Facebook not IG/TikTok

title: Capturing attention in feed: The science behind effective video creative
authors: Facebook IQ (tests by Fors Marsh Group, commissioned by Facebook)
key_findings: (As reported) people spend on average 1.7 s with a piece of mobile feed content vs 2.5 s on desktop; recall significant after 0.25 s exposure
practical_applications: Hook must be readable within the first 1-2 s
limitations: Industry-commissioned; method not public; 2016 Facebook feed

title: Thai Timed Text Style Guide
authors: Netflix
key_findings: Thai subtitles: max 17 cps adult (13 children); SDH 20/17
35 characters per line excluding tone marks and upper/lower vowels; max two lines; prefer one line; bottom-heavy pyramid; avoid two short lines
No sentence-final periods; separate sentences with a single space
practical_applications: Caption timing and layout rules for Thai story clips
limitations: Industry practice, not empirical research; page revision date unknown

title: Timed Text Style Guide: General Requirements
authors: Netflix
key_findings: (Search summary) Minimum subtitle duration 5/6 s (~0.83 s), maximum 7 s
practical_applications: Each caption cue stays at least ~0.8 s
limitations: Not opened directly

title: Bridging cultures through letters: Typotheque's typographic journey in Thailand (with ATypI 2025 talk summary)
authors: Typotheque / Granshan
key_findings: (As reported) a Chulalongkorn study (180+ readers) found looped Thai improved paragraph reading speed; an ATypI 2025 study found no performance difference but all ages perceived looped fonts as more legible; younger readers associate loopless with modernity
practical_applications: Prefer looped Thai fonts for long dialogue/subtitles (weak evidence)
limitations: Foundry-produced summaries; peer-reviewed originals not located

title: How many words do we read per minute? A review and meta-analysis of reading rate
authors: Marc Brysbaert
key_findings: (Search summary) 190 studies: average adult English silent reading 238 wpm non-fiction, 260 fiction; wpm depends on word length so cross-language wpm comparisons are not valid
practical_applications: Do not import English wpm targets into Thai captions
limitations: Search summary only; no Thai data

title: Cross-linguistic investigations of oral and silent reading
authors: Christophe Coupe; Yoon Mi Oh; Francois Pellegrino; Egidio Marsico
key_findings: Eight languages including Thai: oral and silent reading rates are well correlated, suggesting syllabic complexity affects both
practical_applications: Candidate source for Thai reading-rate figures (next research)
limitations: Abstract only; Thai figures not extracted
